34.0.big: Animals reproduce either by copying themselves (asexual) or by combining gametes from two parents (sexual). Then a single cell develops into a whole body.
points: This chapter covers reproduction methods, fertilization, human reproductive anatomy and hormones, embryo development, and pregnancy.

34.1.big: Asexual reproduction makes identical copies fast. Sexual reproduction makes unique offspring that handle change better.
points: Asexual types: fission (splitting in two), budding (an outgrowth breaks off, like hydra), fragmentation (body breaks into pieces that each regrow, like sea stars), parthenogenesis (an unfertilized egg develops, as in some lizards and bees). It's best in a stable environment.
Sexual reproduction mixes genes for diversity, so it's better in a changing environment, even though it costs more energy and needs a mate.
Hermaphroditism: one animal has both male and female parts (earthworms, slugs). Useful when moving around to find a mate is hard.
Sex determination: mammals XX = female, XY = male. Birds ZW = female, ZZ = male. In some reptiles, egg temperature decides sex.

34.2.big: Fertilization happens either outside the body (usually in water) or inside it.
points: External fertilization: eggs and sperm are released into water at the same time (spawning, often cued by temperature or day length). Lots of gametes, mixing of genes, but most offspring die.
Internal fertilization: sperm delivered inside the female. Fewer offspring but better survival, and the female can choose her mate. Some invertebrates store sperm in a spermatheca.

Egg development: oviparity (eggs laid outside, fed by yolk: birds, most reptiles), ovoviparity (eggs kept inside until they hatch: some sharks, snakes), viviparity (young develop inside, fed by the mother: most mammals).
Birds, reptiles and amphibians use a cloaca: one opening for waste and reproduction. Mating is a "cloacal kiss".
Amniotes (reptiles, birds, mammals) have eggs with protective membranes that let them reproduce on land.

34.3.big: Human reproductive organs make gametes (sperm or eggs) by meiosis, and support fertilization and pregnancy.
points: Male: the testes (in the scrotum, kept cooler) make sperm in seminiferous tubules, supported by Sertoli cells. The interstitial cells of Leydig make testosterone. Semen = sperm + fluid from the seminal vesicles (most of it), prostate gland and bulbourethral gland. The penis delivers it.

Female: ovaries hold the eggs. The oviduct (fallopian tube) has cilia that sweep the egg along, and is where fertilization usually happens. The uterus holds the embryo. The vagina is the birth canal. External parts: labia majora, labia minora, clitoris (same embryonic origin as the penis).
Spermatogenesis: one cell → 4 sperm, all the time after puberty.
Oogenesis: one cell → 1 egg (plus small polar bodies), so the egg keeps most of the cytoplasm. Starts before birth and pauses until puberty.

34.4.big: Hormones from the hypothalamus, pituitary and gonads control sperm production and the monthly cycle.
points: The hypothalamus releases gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) → the pituitary releases follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH).
Males: FSH → Sertoli cells (sperm production, and they release inhibin to slow FSH). LH → Leydig cells → testosterone. Testosterone shuts down GnRH, FSH and LH (negative feedback).

The ovarian cycle: follicular phase (FSH grows follicles, which make estrogen/estradiol) → high estradiol triggers an LH surge (positive feedback) → ovulation (egg released, about day 14) → luteal phase (the leftover follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which makes progesterone).
The menstrual cycle (uterus): estrogen rebuilds the lining, progesterone thickens it for implantation. No pregnancy → the corpus luteum breaks down → hormones drop → the lining sheds (menstruation).
Menopause (around age 50): the follicles run out and stop responding to FSH and LH, so estrogen and progesterone fall.

34.5.big: Fertilization makes a diploid zygote, which divides into a hollow ball and then folds into three tissue layers.
points: Fertilization: the sperm binds the zona pellucida (egg coat). The acrosomal reaction releases enzymes that digest a path. Changes to the egg then block polyspermy (more than one sperm getting in). Sperm + egg = diploid zygote.
Cleavage: fast divisions with no growth, so the cell number rises but the cells get smaller. Holoblastic = complete division (little yolk). Meroblastic = partial (lots of yolk, like birds).
Mammals form a blastocyst: the inner cell mass (becomes the embryo; source of embryonic stem cells) and the trophoblast (becomes part of the placenta).
Gastrulation: cells move inward to form three germ layers. Ectoderm (skin, nervous system), mesoderm (muscle, bone, blood, heart), endoderm (gut lining, liver, lungs).
34.5.tip: Ecto = Exterior (skin and nerves). Endo = iNside (gut). Meso = Middle (muscle, bone, blood).

34.6.big: Organogenesis turns the three germ layers into organs, following a body plan set by genes.
points: The notochord (mesoderm) signals the ectoderm above it to fold into the neural plate, then the neural tube (brain and spinal cord). Problems closing it cause spina bifida (bottom) or brain defects (top).
Mesoderm forms somites, blocks that become the vertebrae, back muscles and skin.
Axes (head-to-tail, back-to-belly, left-right) are set by genes and gradients of signaling molecules (Hox genes, Wnt).

34.7.big: Human pregnancy (gestation) lasts about 38 weeks in three trimesters, and birth is driven by positive feedback.
points: The embryo releases human beta chorionic gonadotropin (β-HCG) (what pregnancy tests detect), which keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone. Later the placenta takes over making progesterone.
First trimester: major organs form (most sensitive time); morning sickness is common. Second and third: growth.
Labor: oxytocin → contractions → more oxytocin (positive feedback). Stage 1: the cervix thins and opens to about 10 cm. Stage 2: the baby is delivered. Stage 3: the placenta is delivered.
Contraception: barrier methods, hormones (pills, implants: the most effective short-term options, which block GnRH and so FSH and LH), and surgery.
Infertility causes: STDs scarring the tubes, blocked tubes, hormone problems, stress, age. Treatments include IVF (egg and sperm combined in a dish, embryo implanted).
